summary:
GeoTrends Uganda is an interactive web app that helps users explore how Uganda's farming seasons are changing and where those changes are happening.

Using 27 years (1999–2025) of daily NASA POWER rainfall, temperature and soil moisture data, we developed a system that tracks eight climate variables important to agriculture, including when the rains start, how long dry spells last, how many rainy days occur and how intense the rainfall is. The results are organised across eight farming zones and three seasons, allowing users to explore trends on an interactive map, view statistical evidence and compare different regions.

One of our key findings is that rainfall intensity has increased across all eight farming zones, while rainy days have decreased during the March–May season around Lake Victoria and in the Cattle Corridor.

This matters because agriculture in Uganda depends heavily on rainfall. Changes in the timing and distribution of rain can affect planting decisions, soil conditions and harvests. By turning complex climate data into clear, locally relevant evidence, GeoTrends Uganda aims to help farmers, agricultural extension workers and planners better understand these changes and make more informed decisions.
details:
GeoTrends Uganda

What the project does and how it works

GeoTrends Uganda is a web application that helps us understand whether Uganda's farming seasons are changing over time, and where those changes are happening. We wanted to go beyond simply looking at whether rainfall or temperatures are increasing or decreasing. Instead, we wanted to understand what these changes actually mean for farmers: Are the rains starting later? Are dry spells becoming longer? Is rainfall becoming more intense? Are temperatures getting unusually high?

To answer these questions, we built a system that analyses historical climate data and presents the results through an interactive map and dashboard.

We started by collecting daily data from NASA POWER for the period 1999–2025, covering rainfall (PRECTOTCORR), maximum air temperature (T2M_MAX) and root-zone soil moisture (GWETROOT). The data covers Uganda on a 0.5° × 0.625° grid.

Using Python, we processed this data to calculate eight farming-related climate variables for each year, season and grid cell. These include total seasonal rainfall, the start and length of each rainy season, the longest dry spell, the number of rainy days, rainfall intensity, unusually hot days and soil moisture.

One important decision was not to treat Uganda as having one uniform rainfall calendar. We divided the country into eight farming zones based on its agro-ecological regions. Each zone has its own seasonal calendar, reflecting the differences between the north, south and central parts of the country. For example, the south and centre generally experience two main rainy seasons, while the north has one longer rainy season. We also excluded grid cells covering lakes.

After processing the data, we tested 168 climate time series (eight zones, three seasons and eight variables) to determine whether meaningful trends exist. We used the Mann-Kendall test with the Hamed–Rao correction to account for consecutive wet or dry years, Sen's slope to measure the rate of change, and the Pettitt test to investigate whether changes happened gradually or around a particular point in time. Out of the 168 trends, 79 were statistically significant at p < 0.05.

We then brought these results together in the GeoTrends Uganda web app. Users can select a farming season and climate variable to explore the results on an interactive map. Zones are highlighted only when a statistically significant trend is detected, with red and blue indicating whether the change is potentially worse or better for farming. Each zone also has its own case file containing charts, trend measurements, p-values and explanations in plain language. We included an evidence board as well, allowing users to compare all eight zones and their climate variables at once.

Benefits and intended impact

Agriculture in Uganda depends heavily on rainfall, which means that changes in when rain arrives, how often it falls and how intensely it falls can have a real impact on farming.

We believe one of the biggest benefits of GeoTrends Uganda is that it makes climate information easier to understand and use. Rather than presenting people with large datasets or complicated statistical results, the app turns those results into information that can help explain what is happening in different parts of the country.

One of our most interesting findings is that rainfall intensity has increased during the rainy seasons across all eight farming zones. We also found fewer rainy days during the March–May season around Lake Victoria and in the Cattle Corridor. This suggests that, in some areas, rain is falling in heavier bursts but on fewer days. Such changes can increase surface runoff and soil erosion while reducing the amount of water that has time to soak into the soil.

Our intended impact is to make this kind of information useful to people working in agriculture, including agricultural extension officers, district planners, researchers and students. It could help inform decisions about planting calendars, soil conservation and water management. More broadly, we hope the project encourages people to use local evidence when thinking about how agriculture can adapt to a changing climate.

What makes the project creative

What makes GeoTrends Uganda different is how we approached the problem. We didn't want to create another dashboard showing average rainfall and temperature. We wanted to connect climate data to the actual conditions farmers experience.

There were a few things that shaped our approach:

  • Looking beyond averages: We developed variables that capture practical farming conditions, such as delayed rainy-season starts, longer dry spells, fewer rainy days and more intense rainfall.
  • Recognising regional differences: Instead of applying the same rainfall calendar across Uganda, we gave each farming zone its own seasonal calendar. This makes the analysis more relevant to the different conditions across the country.
  • Questioning the data, not just analysing it: During our initial analysis, which covered 1984–2025, we noticed that rainfall, temperature and soil moisture all showed an unusual jump around 1998 across much of Uganda. Independent satellite sunlight data did not show a similar change. This raised concerns that we were seeing a change in the underlying data rather than an actual climate event. We investigated this and decided to begin our analysis in 1999. We also documented this decision on the app's Method page so users can understand why we made it.
  • Making the results meaningful: The map doesn't simply show whether a value increased or decreased. It considers whether that change is potentially beneficial or harmful to farming. We also designed the interface to make the statistical results understandable to people without a background in climate science.

Factors we considered

Throughout development, we had to make several decisions to ensure that our results were as reliable and useful as possible.

Data reliability: We investigated the unusual 1998 data break before settling on our analysis period. We also considered the fact that reanalysis datasets can record frequent light rainfall. To avoid counting very small amounts of rain as meaningful rainy days, we used a threshold of at least 2 mm per day instead of 1 mm. We also acknowledge the limitations of MERRA-2 temperature data over Uganda and flag this in the application.

Statistical reliability: We didn't want to mistake normal year-to-year fluctuations for long-term climate changes. We therefore used statistical tests that account for consecutive wet and dry years and reported both the significance of a trend and the size of the change. We also considered multiple testing: with 168 separate tests, some results could appear significant by chance. We make this limitation clear rather than presenting every significant result as definitive.

Local relevance: We considered Uganda's different agro-ecological regions, seasonal rainfall patterns and farming conditions. We also excluded lake-covered grid cells to avoid including irrelevant observations in the farming zones.

Accessibility: We wanted the application to be useful beyond people who work with climate data. We used straightforward explanations, interactive charts and a red-blue colour scheme with neutral grey to help distinguish the results, including for users with colour-vision deficiencies.

Limitations: NASA POWER data has a spatial resolution of roughly 55 km, meaning the results represent broader regional patterns rather than conditions on an individual farm. We also recognise that identifying a rainfall or temperature trend does not automatically prove that crop yields or farmer incomes have changed.

Tools and technologies used

We used a combination of data analysis tools and modern web technologies to build the project.

  • Data sources: NASA POWER API for daily rainfall, temperature and soil moisture data; Natural Earth datasets for country boundaries and lakes.
  • Data processing and statistical analysis: Python, NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, Shapely and Requests.
  • Testing: pytest for testing the data-processing pipeline.
  • Web application: TypeScript, React and Vite.
  • Visualisation and mapping: MapLibre GL, deck.gl and Observable Plot.
  • Interface and animation: Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion.
  • Statistical implementation: We also ported the statistical calculations to TypeScript to support the web application.
  • Deployment and collaboration: GitHub and Vercel.
  • AI-assisted development: Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT helped us during parts of the development process.

Ultimately, GeoTrends Uganda is our attempt to make climate data more meaningful at a local level. We wanted to build something that doesn't just tell people that the climate is changing, but helps them explore what is changing, where it is happening and why it matters for agriculture in Uganda.
